Family Health

Osteoarthritis: diagnosis, joint-specific care and treatment options

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Osteoarthritis can affect far more than the appearance of a joint on a scan. It may make gripping a cup, climbing stairs, walking or turning your head uncomfortable. There is no single treatment that restores every affected joint to its earlier state, but a tailored plan can improve pain, movement and daily life. The plan should fit the joints involved and the activities that matter to you.

What a diagnosis does and does not mean

Osteoarthritis involves changes in cartilage and other joint tissues. It often develops gradually, but symptoms and progression differ between people. Some have mild or intermittent discomfort; others have substantial pain and reduced function.

It is more common with increasing age, although younger adults can develop it after injury or because of other joint factors. It is not simply proof that you have used your body too much.

A scan taken for an unrelated injury may show joint changes, but early osteoarthritis is not usually diagnosed only after a fracture. Some early changes are not visible on an X-ray, and the amount of change on a scan does not tell the whole story about pain or disability.

How osteoarthritis is assessed

Assessment begins with the history and an examination. Explain which joints hurt, whether pain follows activity, how long stiffness lasts and what movements or everyday tasks have become difficult. Previous injury, swelling and other health conditions can help the clinician distinguish the cause.

A typical pattern can often be diagnosed without imaging. An X-ray may be useful when the presentation is unusual or another problem is suspected. MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to show soft tissues as well as bones, but it is not a routine requirement for every painful joint.

Blood tests do not confirm osteoarthritis. They may help investigate another explanation, including inflammatory arthritis. A sample of joint fluid may be examined when infection or crystal arthritis, such as gout, is a concern. These tests answer specific questions rather than forming a checklist everyone needs.

Exercise is a central part of care

A useful programme combines appropriate strengthening, movement or stretching exercises and general physical activity. Gentle stretching can help stiffness and preserve movement in affected knees, hips or the back, but stretching alone does not replace strengthening.

Start at a manageable level and build gradually. Walking, cycling or water-based activity may suit some people. A physiotherapist can adapt movements to pain, balance, other illnesses and the demands of work or caring for a child.

Some discomfort can occur when beginning exercise. Severe or escalating pain, marked swelling, giving way or new neurological symptoms call for review rather than simply pushing harder. The aim is consistent, sustainable activity, with adjustments when needed.

Heat, cold, massage and complementary approaches

A comfortably warm or cool pack may ease symptoms temporarily. Protect the skin and avoid extreme temperatures, particularly if sensation is reduced. A warm bath can also be relaxing, but adding Epsom salts has not been established as a way to reverse joint damage.

Massage may offer short-term comfort, although the research is limited. Physiotherapy has a different role: it can provide an assessed exercise and function programme rather than being grouped with herbal remedies.

Acupuncture recommendations differ. NCCIH describes possible modest or short-lived symptom benefits, while NICE recommends against offering acupuncture or dry needling for osteoarthritis. It should not be presented as a cure or a substitute for active rehabilitation.

Before paying for a complementary treatment, ask what outcome it is meant to improve, how strong the evidence is and when to stop if it is not helping. Discuss herbs and supplements with the care team because natural products can still cause adverse effects or interact with medicines.

Food, weight and supplement claims

A varied diet supports general health. When weight management is appropriate, a sustainable plan may reduce stress on weight-bearing joints and improve symptoms. This is a supportive option, not a reason to blame a person for having arthritis.

Fruit and vegetables provide compounds including flavonoids and antioxidants. Research into inflammation is interesting, but it does not establish a particular flavonoid-rich menu as a dependable treatment for knee osteoarthritis or prove that it repairs cartilage.

Vitamin C, vitamin D, beta-carotene and omega-3 fats have nutritional roles. Getting suitable amounts is different from taking extra doses to treat osteoarthritis. Evidence from rheumatoid arthritis or another inflammatory condition should not automatically be applied to osteoarthritis.

Fish oil, ginger and green tea are sometimes promoted for joint symptoms. Food or ordinary drinks differ from concentrated extracts, and the evidence is not strong enough to promise relief or disease reversal for everyone. Check supplements, especially if you take regular medicines, are pregnant or are breastfeeding.

When hands and wrists are affected

Hand osteoarthritis commonly affects the joints nearest the fingernails, the middle finger joints and the base of the thumb where it meets the wrist. Arthritis can also affect the wrist itself, sometimes following injury or because of an inflammatory condition.

Symptoms can include pain, stiffness, swelling, weaker grip and reduced finger movement. Some people notice grinding or crackling, called crepitus, when moving a joint. Grasping a pan, opening a jar or fastening clothes may become difficult.

Redness can accompany irritation, but a suddenly hot, very swollen joint should not be assumed to be ordinary osteoarthritis. Women are more likely to have osteoarthritis, particularly later in life; that does not mean every woman develops hand symptoms earlier than men.

An occupational or hand therapist may suggest grip aids, adapted tools, pacing or selected splints. Medicines, injections and sometimes surgery are considered according to the joints involved and the effect on daily function.

Osteoarthritis of the hip

One or both hips may be affected. Pain can be felt in the groin, thigh or buttock and sometimes referred to the knee. Stiffness may make it harder to bend, put on shoes or walk comfortably.

Having symptoms in one hip rather than both does not reliably distinguish osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis or another condition. Examination and the overall clinical picture are needed.

Many people manage hip symptoms with exercise, physiotherapy, suitable pain treatment and, when helpful, a correctly fitted walking aid. If symptoms continue to substantially limit life, specialist discussion may include injections or hip replacement. Surgery is not an inevitable next step for everyone.

Osteoarthritis of the knee

Knee osteoarthritis can affect one or both knees. Age, family history and previous joint injury can contribute. Pain, stiffness or a feeling of instability may change how you climb stairs, stand up or walk.

Repeated high loads and injuries can matter, but a blanket statement that running or tennis inevitably causes knee osteoarthritis is misleading. The effect of an activity depends on training, injury history, symptoms and individual capacity.

Varying activity and strengthening the muscles supporting the knee can help avoid repeatedly loading the same structures in the same way. A clinician or physiotherapist can help adjust a routine rather than advising everyone to stop sport. Treatment is guided by pain and function as well as joint changes.

When a knee brace may help

A brace may help selected people with instability or an uneven loading pattern. Some designs shift load away from a painful part of the knee; others provide support. It is not automatically the best treatment for every swollen or painful knee.

NICE recommends considering supports selectively when exercise is ineffective or unsuitable without them and an aid is likely to improve movement. Fit, comfort and the purpose of the device should be reviewed.

An off-the-shelf sleeve and a fitted unloading brace are not equivalent. Ask which type, if any, suits the problem and the activities you want to do. Persistent skin irritation, new pain or a poor fit needs attention.

Neck changes and cervical spondylosis

Cervical spondylosis describes age-related changes in the discs and joints of the neck. AAOS estimates that these changes affect more than 85% of people over 60, but many have no noticeable symptoms. A common scan finding is not the same as severe disease.

When symptoms occur, they may include neck stiffness, shoulder-blade pain or a headache starting at the back of the head. Pain may extend down an arm or into the fingers. Numbness, tingling or muscle weakness can suggest that a nerve is affected and should be assessed.

New walking or balance difficulty, sudden loss of coordination or new loss of bladder or bowel control needs emergency assessment. Do not try to manage these changes with neck stretches or massage while waiting for a routine appointment.

For uncomplicated symptoms, treatment may involve adapted activity, exercises, physiotherapy and suitable medicines. Surgery is considered for particular nerve or spinal-cord problems, not simply because an X-ray shows age-related changes.

Osteoarthritis and lower-back symptoms

Osteoarthritis can affect the small facet joints at the back of the spine and contribute to stiffness or pain. Aging and previous injury may play a part, and higher body weight or repeated mechanical strain can influence symptoms and risk.

A sedentary job or back pain alone does not establish the diagnosis. Back pain has many causes, and the location and pattern of symptoms matter. Reduced movement, tenderness or stiffness may occur, but weakness, numbness or tingling needs assessment for possible nerve involvement.

The condition does not inevitably worsen into severe disability if a particular treatment is not started. Symptoms can fluctuate. Seek urgent help for new bladder or bowel problems, loss of feeling around the groin or rapidly developing leg weakness; these need assessment beyond an osteoarthritis label.

Reducing avoidable strain and injury

Age and inherited susceptibility cannot be changed, and no programme guarantees prevention. Useful steps include reducing avoidable injuries, varying repetitive loads and building strength appropriate to your activities.

For sport, choose suitable footwear and equipment, allow recovery and progress training sensibly. A support should have a specific purpose; it is not a guarantee that an injury or arthritis will be prevented.

Balanced nutrition, sufficient sleep and a supported approach to weight can help overall health and coping. If you have diabetes, follow your usual glucose-management plan. That is important for health, but should not be advertised as a proven way to prevent all osteoarthritis.

Medicines, injections and surgery

Pain treatment can make activity easier. Depending on the joint and your health, a clinician may consider an anti-inflammatory gel or an oral medicine. Tablets require attention to stomach, kidney and heart risks, interactions and pregnancy or breastfeeding.

A corticosteroid injection into an affected joint may provide temporary relief in selected cases. It does not rebuild cartilage. Discuss expected benefit, duration, possible harms and whether it will help you participate in rehabilitation.

When substantial pain or loss of function persists despite suitable nonsurgical care, an orthopedic assessment may consider joint replacement or another procedure. Decisions should reflect symptoms, goals, overall health and the likely benefits and risks, rather than a scan score alone.

Follow-up and the longer-term outlook

Osteoarthritis is a long-term condition, but a diagnosis does not mean that meaningful improvement is impossible. Review goals such as walking a little farther, sleeping more comfortably or managing an important daily task.

Agree when to reassess the plan, especially if a new medicine, brace or exercise programme is started. Bring questions about side effects, practical barriers and the activities you still find difficult.

A suddenly hot, markedly swollen joint with fever or inability to bear weight needs prompt medical assessment. New neurological or bladder/bowel symptoms need urgent attention. A known diagnosis should never be used to dismiss a new and different problem.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Assessment usually begins with symptoms and examination; scans and tests are selected for a clinical reason.

Tailored exercise and practical support are central to care.

A brace, injection or operation is an individual decision, not a universal sequence.

Complementary approaches and nutrition claims need evidence checks; no supplement is a proven cure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you keep a note of symptoms, activities that are difficult and questions for an appointment. It cannot diagnose arthritis from a pain record or replace an individualized rehabilitation plan.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for a suddenly hot, swollen joint or inability to bear weight. New walking or coordination problems, bladder/bowel changes, saddle numbness or rapidly developing weakness require urgent or emergency assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A useful care plan is based on symptoms and function, not just scan findings.
  • Hands, hips, knees, neck and back may need different adaptations.
  • Exercise should be tailored and progressed, not abandoned automatically.
  • Food and supplements cannot be promised to repair cartilage.
  • New severe or neurological symptoms should not be attributed to ordinary arthritis without assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a complete cure for osteoarthritis?

There is no single treatment that reverses all joint changes. Exercise, symptom treatment, aids and selected surgery can still make a major difference to comfort and function.

Do I need an MRI or blood tests?

Not routinely. A typical diagnosis may be made from symptoms and an examination. Imaging, blood tests or joint-fluid analysis are used when they can answer a specific question or investigate another cause.

Should I stop exercising if I have knee arthritis?

Usually the aim is to adapt activity and strengthen the supporting muscles. Some initial discomfort can occur, but significant worsening, swelling or instability needs review. A physiotherapist can help choose a suitable programme.

Will fish oil, ginger, green tea or Epsom salts cure it?

No. These should not be promised to reverse osteoarthritis. Some comfort measures may help symptoms, but supplement evidence is limited and concentrated products may interact with medicines.

Is acupuncture recommended?

Recommendations differ. Some evidence summaries describe modest temporary pain relief, while NICE advises against offering it for osteoarthritis. Discuss local guidance, cost and realistic expectations without replacing exercise-based care.

Does everybody with knee osteoarthritis need a brace?

No. A brace is most useful when it addresses a specific loading or stability problem and improves function. The type and fit should be assessed rather than chosen simply because the knee hurts.

Does pain in both hips mean rheumatoid arthritis?

No. Osteoarthritis can affect one or both hips, and laterality alone cannot identify the arthritis type. The clinician considers symptoms, examination and any appropriate tests.

When are neck or back symptoms an emergency?

New loss of bladder or bowel control, new walking or coordination problems, saddle numbness or rapidly developing weakness needs urgent or emergency assessment. Do not wait to see whether home remedies help.

Can diet prevent osteoarthritis getting worse?

Balanced nutrition and appropriate weight management can support health and symptoms. No particular food, antioxidant dose or vitamin supplement has been established as a universal way to stop progression.

When might joint replacement be considered?

When symptoms substantially affect quality of life and appropriate nonsurgical care is ineffective or unsuitable. A specialist helps weigh the likely benefit, risks and personal goals.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
